meaning: The three-chord family of tonic, subdominant and dominant, as I-IV-V-I, I-IV-I-V or I-IV-V-IV. It is the most common loop in folk, blues, country and rock and roll.
The chords I, V, vi and IV, with vi minor and the others major, in any rotation. The same chords read in minor as i-bVI-bIII-bVII, and the mood depends on which chord feels like home.
I-vi-IV-V, the doo-wop loop of the 1950s, still common in pop.
I-bVII-IV, three major chords that borrow the flat seventh of the Mixolydian mode. It is common in folk and blues.
i-bVII-bVI-bVII, a minor chord that shuttles between the flat seventh and flat sixth. Heard in hard rock and trap.
ii7-V7-Imaj7 in major, or iim7b5-V7alt-i in minor. It is the staple of jazz, deep house, lo-fi and R&B.
I-IV-vi-V, a cousin of the 50s loop that swaps the order of the last chords. It appears mostly in chord sheets.
i-iv-bVII-bIII, a minor loop built around the minor fourth-degree chord. Heard in house and soul.
i-bIII-bVII-bVI, a minor loop on the first, third, seventh and sixth degrees. It appears mostly in chord sheets.
I-iii-IV-V, a major loop with a minor chord on the third degree. It appears mostly in chord sheets.
i-v-bVI-bVII, a minor loop with a minor fifth-degree chord. Heard in synthwave.
IV-V-iii-vi, played as IVmaj7-V7-iii7-vi7: the loop of Japanese pop and city pop. Its minor form is bVImaj7-bVII7-v7-i.
i-bVII-bVI-V, a falling minor line that ends on a major dominant. In its Phrygian reading it is iv-III-bII-I.
bVI-bVII-I, often continued to IV: a cadence-style loop from video game music, rock and pop.
Twelve bars of dominant sevenths: I I I I, IV IV I I, V IV I V. Variants are the quick change, the shuffle ending, the minor form (i7 iv7 bVI7 V7) and bebop.
I-vi-ii-V, the jazz turnaround that leads back to the tonic. Heard in jazz and lo-fi.
I-V-vi-iii-IV-I-IV-V, an eight-chord cycle over a stepwise falling bass. Heard in pop.
bII-i, a major chord a semitone above the minor tonic. It sounds menacing in metal, trap and drill.
IV-iv-I, a major subdominant that turns minor before the tonic.
iv-bVII-bIII-bVI, a minor loop heard in trance.
iv7-bVII7-Imaj7, Fm7, Bb7 and Cmaj7 in C: the minor four and the flat-seven dominant reach the tonic from below. It rests on search excerpts and is not checked against a full source.
vi-ii-V-I, a chain of fifths that runs down to the tonic. It rests on search excerpts and is not checked against a full source.
Main loop i-VI-III-VII (Am-F-C-G), two bars per chord over an eight-bar loop. Other loops are iv-VII-III-VI and i-III-VII-VI, played as triads plus minor sevenths and suspended chords.
Main loop ii-V-I with minor sevenths, sevenths, major sevenths and ninths, one chord per bar. Other loops are i9-IV13 and an Am7-Dm7 vamp over two bars, voiced low and wide across two octaves.
Main loop I-IV-V, one chord per bar, with short mid-range stabs on slots 2, 6, 10 and 14. Other loops are Am7-Dm7, i-VI-III-VII and ii-V-i.

Main loop ii9-V9-Imaj9, a bar or more per chord, rootless minor ninths held, rolled, comped or broken. Other loops are IVmaj7-iii7-ii7-Imaj7, Imaj9-vi9-ii9-V9, Imaj7-vi7-ii7-V7, Imaj7-IVmaj7 and i9-VImaj7-IIImaj7-VII.
Often one chord or none. Dub techno stabs a single minor seventh, and when the chord moves it changes every two or four bars.

One to three minor chords, one per bar, with the 808 taking the root and the upper tones high, arpeggiated and widely spaced. Main loop i-bVI-bVII; others are i, i-iv, i-bVII-bVI, i-VI-VII-i, i-bVI-V and i-III-VI-VII.
Main loop i-iv-VI-VII, two bars per chord. A second loop is i9-IV13.
Main loop vi-IV-I-V with sevenths and ninths. A second loop is I-V-vi-IV in the same dress.
Main loop ii9-V13-Imaj9, a bar or more per chord. Other ideas are quartal drift and planing Imaj7#11 to bVIImaj7#11.
Liquid drum and bass uses i-VI-III-VII or ii7-V7-I-vi7. Neurofunk uses i-iv-i-v.
Pop leans on I-V-vi-IV, the axis loop.
Main loop i-bVI-bIII-bVII, with chromatic mediants, pedal tones and open fifths.
A big room loop of i-i-VI-VI.
Main loop i-bVII-IV; a second loop is i-v-bVI-bVII.
Main loop i-bVI-bVII; a second loop is bII-i.
How long each chord lasts. In a chart set most bars hold one chord, and runs of 2 and 4 beats lead. A chord note lasts two to eight beats.
Borrowing chords from the parallel minor into a major key: iv, bVI (8), bVII (10), bIII (3) and ii diminished (2). Only bIII, bVI and bVII move the root a semitone off the major scale.
A chord whose root lies 3, 4, 8 or 9 semitones from the last root, with the same quality and one common tone. Diatonic mediants share two tones.

A chord of the opposite quality that shares no tone with the first. From a major chord its root lies 3 or 8 semitones up (C major to Eb minor or Ab minor), and from a minor chord 4 or 9 (C minor to E major or A major).
